To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

African American and Hispanic OB/ GYNs and OB/ GYN practices with increasing patient population diversity were more knowledgeable of and concerned about CVD disparities, but OB/ GYN knowledge, attitudes, practice patterns, and barriers to CVD prevention and care varied by race and ethnicity.

OB/GYNs with more minority patients were more knowledgeable of racial/ethnic disparities, and that the most commonly cited barriers to CVD counseling and care were patient nonadherence, time constraints, and inadequate training.
OB/GYN race and practice demographics predicted differences in OB-GYNs’ knowledge of, attitudes toward, and practice patterns related to racial/ethnic CVD disparities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the racial/ethnic disparities that exist in the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease (CWD).
the role of OB/GYNs in reducing CVD disparities in women.
racial and ethnic disparities in cardiovascular disease (C.V.D.) and its risk factors, and the role that obstetrician–gynaecologists (ob/gyns) play in addressing these disparities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
OB/GYNs are aware of the disparities in CVD and are willing to address the issue with their patients, but are limited by their training and the time constraints of their practice.

OB/GYN race and ethnicity as well as OB/GYN practices’ minority population may be related to OB/GYNs knowledge, attitude, and practice patterns in regards to racial and ethnic disparities in cardiovascular disease.

African American and Hispanic OB-GYNs and OB-GYN practices with increasing patient populations of African American and Hispanic women have greater knowledge of CVD disparities, are more concerned with the risk of CVD in these groups, and have greater knowledge of the risk factors for CVD in these populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
OB/GYNs are knowledgeable and concerned with racial/ethnic disparities but are not always translating that knowledge into practice.
African American OB/GYNs were more knowledgeable and concerned about CVD risk in African American and Hispanic women than their White counterparts.

OB/GYNs are knowledgeable about the increased CVD risk of minority women, but are less concerned with Hispanic women than with African American women, and that OB/GYN practices in minority populations may have a greater awareness of the increased CVD risks in these patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
OB/GYNs need to be aware of the racial/ethnic CVD disparities and to be more proactive in addressing the disparities in their practices.
there are significant disparities in CVD among racial and ethnic groups.
OB/GYNs need more information about CVD risk factors and preventive strategies in minority women, especially in Hispanics.
